clue.text: Really perfect foxtrot compensates for earlier tango

indicators.note: to compensate for something is to make up for it, so one letter stands in where another used to be

parts.note: perfect in the sense of whole and undamaged
F in the NATO phonetic alphabet
T in the NATO alphabet; 'earlier' picks the first of the two in the word for perfect

explanation.surface: A dancer's flawless foxtrot makes up for a poor tango earlier in the competition.
explanation.walkthrough: INTACT has two Ts; 'earlier' says the first one goes, and F takes its place to give IN FACT.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are sentence adverbs used for emphasis or to confirm truth, as in 'it was, in fact, true' and 'it was really true'.

clue.text: Balloon delayed visiting France previously

indicators.note: something done previously comes first, so this part is placed ahead of the other

parts.note: someone visiting a place is in it
F is the international vehicle code for France
a delayed train is late

explanation.surface: A hot-air balloon flight in France has been held up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balloon' looks like a noun, but it is the verb, to swell up. 'Previously' moves the France-visiting part ahead of the delay.
explanation.definitionFit: To balloon is to swell or expand rapidly, which is exactly what to inflate means as a verb.

clue.text: Much ado about nothing next to Conservative centre

indicators.note: about means around, so the shortened word wraps around the pair
much of something is most but not all of it, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: ado is fuss or commotion; shortened it loses its last S

indicators.note: placing one thing next to another puts them side by side in sequence

parts.note: nothing as the figure zero, shaped like an O
C is the standard abbreviation for Conservative

explanation.surface: A political commentator scoffs at a great fuss over nothing at Conservative party headquarters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Much ado about nothing' looks like the Shakespeare title; it splits into most of FUSS around O and C.
explanation.definitionFit: A focus is the central point of attention or activity, so it serves as a synonym for centre.

clue.text: Bar Merriam-Webster's latest, really wants Chambers

indicators.note: bar here means except or excluding, so a letter is left out

parts.note: to crave is to want something badly

indicators.note: the latest of a sequence is the final one, so only the last letter is wanted

parts.note: the final letter of the dictionary's name

explanation.surface: A lexicographer at the rival American dictionary really wishes they had the Chambers dictionary instead.
explanation.walkthrough: Merriam-Webster and Chambers are both dictionaries, so 'Chambers' looks like a book title; it is plain rooms. 'Bar' means except: CRAVES without R.
explanation.definitionFit: Caves are hollow underground spaces, natural rooms, so they fit as a synonym for chambers.

clue.text: Good way to interrupt relative's rhetorical devices

indicators.note: to interrupt is to break into the middle of something, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: SIS is short for sister, a relative
a good way is a long distance, and a mile is the measure

explanation.surface: A family member's speeches are full of figures of speech, and someone suggests a good way to stop them.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is read as 'is' joining wordplay to definition, not as a possessive. 'A good way' is the idiom for a long distance, measured here in one unit.
explanation.definitionFit: A simile compares two things using like or as, one of the standard figures of speech in rhetoric.

clue.text: Cut breaking news channel, it's slapdash

indicators.note: something breaking into a whole splits it open and lodges inside

parts.note: Sky News is a British TV news channel
to etch is to cut a design into a surface

explanation.surface: A critic says a news channel's edited breaking-news coverage is careless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breaking news' is a stock phrase, but 'breaking' is the insertion signal. Sky News is a British 24-hour news channel.
explanation.definitionFit: Sketchy work is rough and lacking detail, done hastily, which is what slapdash describes.

clue.text: Guiding light of masculine pop band — former prime minister!

parts.note: M is the standard abbreviation for masculine
A-ha is the Norwegian pop band behind 'Take On Me'
Rishi Sunak, UK prime minister 2022 to 2024

explanation.surface: A boy band's spiritual mentor turns out, surprisingly, to be an ex-prime minister.
explanation.walkthrough: Rishi Sunak was a UK prime minister; A-ha is a 1980s Norwegian band.
explanation.definitionFit: A maharishi is a Hindu sage or spiritual teacher, someone followers look to for guidance, hence a guiding light.

clue.text: Felt Adele broadcast tried to generate interest?

indicators.note: to broadcast seed is to scatter it widely, so the letters are scattered into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: The singer Adele went on the radio and tried to drum up interest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Felt' and 'broadcast' look like a verb and the radio; together with the singer's name they are the letters and the scatter signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Handing out printed flyers door to door is a way of drumming up public interest, hence the question mark for an example.

clue.text: Lean close to Barclays and Lloyds?

indicators.note: the close of something is its end, so only the final letter is taken

parts.note: last letter of the bank's name
Lloyds is a British bank, an example of a lender, hence the question mark

explanation.surface: One British bank leans on, or cosies up to, another.
explanation.walkthrough: Barclays and Lloyds are both major UK banks. 'Lean' looks like a verb but is the adjective meaning thin.
explanation.definitionFit: Lean as an adjective means thin with little fat, which a slender person is.

clue.text: Gains pounds, fifty deposited early

indicators.note: early means sooner in the sequence, so the letter goes back in nearer the start
to deposit something is to put it down, so the letter is lifted out of its spot

parts.note: the heart pounds or pulses
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: Someone banks money, putting in fifty pounds ahead of time, and sees it grow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pounds' looks like money but is the verb, to beat. The L of PULSES is moved earlier, to sit right after the P.
explanation.definitionFit: Pluses are advantages or positive points, and gains as a noun are benefits acquired, so the two are synonyms.

clue.text: Boat race in East London introducing prize, for what it's worth

indicators.note: to introduce something is to bring it in ahead of what follows, so one part leads the other

parts.note: Cockney rhyming slang: boat race means face
to prize something is to value it

explanation.surface: A rowing race in the East End offers a prize, for what it's worth.
explanation.walkthrough: East London is home of Cockney rhyming slang, where 'boat race' stands for face. 'For what it's worth' looks like a throwaway phrase; 'for' is the joining word.
explanation.definitionFit: Face value is the nominal amount printed on a coin, note or ticket, the sum it is officially worth.

clue.text: Cast keep entertaining audience at the back

indicators.note: a host entertaining a guest holds them inside, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: to keep something is to have it

indicators.note: the back of a word is its end, so only its last letter is kept

parts.note: last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A theatre cast keeps the audience in the back rows amused.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast' and 'audience' paint a theatre, but 'Cast' is the verb, to throw.
explanation.definitionFit: To cast and to heave both mean to throw something, especially with effort, as with a line or rope.

clue.text: Promotes uncapped players

indicators.note: with its cap removed something loses its top, so the first letter goes

parts.note: players of the bass guitar or double bass

explanation.surface: A selector gives a chance to players who have not yet won an international cap.
explanation.walkthrough: An uncapped player in sport has never played for their country; here the cap is the first letter of a type of musician.
explanation.definitionFit: To promote something is to help it along or further it, which is to assist it.

clue.text: Dog showed the way after daughter went off

indicators.note: coming after means placed later in the sequence, behind the other part

parts.note: a cur is a mongrel dog
D is the standard abbreviation for daughter
to lead is to show the way

explanation.surface: A family dog led the walk once the daughter had left.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Went off' looks like the daughter leaving; it is the definition, meaning turned sour.
explanation.definitionFit: Milk that has gone off has soured and separated into lumps, which is what curdled means.

clue.text: Pull the plug on the French scheming twenty-four-seven

parts.note: to pull the plug on something is to end it
les is French for the (plural)
sly means cunning or scheming

explanation.surface: Someone wants to scrap the French who scheme around the clock.
explanation.walkthrough: Three plain synonyms run end to end; the French article is plural LES.
explanation.definitionFit: Twenty-four-seven means all day, every day without stopping, which is doing something without end.

clue.text: Manage to split dark pants, dungarees, on vacation — they're tight

indicators.note: to split something is to break it apart and sit in the gap
pants is British slang for rubbish, so the preceding letters are a mess to be rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
to run a business is to manage it

indicators.note: a place on vacation is empty of people, so only the outer letters remain

parts.note: first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: Someone tries to rip their dark trousers and dungarees while on holiday; the clothes are too tight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pants' looks like trousers next to dungarees, but it is British slang for rubbish, the shuffle signal. 'Tight' is British slang for drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Tight is informal for drunk, and drunkards are people habitually intoxicated, so 'they're tight' describes them.

clue.text: Stiff from sweeping, sacrificing technique primarily for power

indicators.note: to sacrifice one thing for another is to give it up in exchange, so one letter is swapped out

parts.note: sweeping changes are wide-ranging, extensive ones

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: first letter of the word
P is the standard abbreviation for power

explanation.surface: A cleaner or curler is stiff from sweeping, giving up technique for brute force.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stiff' looks like aching muscles; it means costly, as in a stiff price.
explanation.definitionFit: A stiff price or fine is a steep, high one, so stiff is an informal synonym for costly.

clue.text: Is backing singer from the East offering his instrument?

indicators.note: backing means moving backwards, so the letters run in the opposite direction

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: in an across answer, reading from the east means reading right to left

parts.note: a rat is an informer, someone who sings to the police

explanation.surface: A backing singer from India brings along their instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing singer' looks like a pop-group role; 'backing' turns round IS and 'from the East' turns round the informer. 'His' points back to an Eastern musician.
explanation.definitionFit: The sitar is the long-necked plucked string instrument of Indian classical music, as played by Ravi Shankar.

clue.text: Best pressure to serve up stout

parts.note: a plum job or role is the best one
P is the standard abbreviation for pressure

explanation.surface: A barman is under pressure to pour the best stout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stout' looks like the dark beer, but it is the adjective meaning fat.
explanation.definitionFit: Stout and plump both describe a person who is rather fat or rounded in build.

clue.text: One placing flags around city for song and dance

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: a paver lays flagstones, or flags, for paths
LA is Los Angeles

explanation.surface: Someone putting up flags around town for a musical show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flags' looks like bunting, but here it is flagstones, so the person is one who paves.
explanation.definitionFit: A song and dance is a needless fuss, and palaver is an informal British word for the same tedious fuss.

clue.text: Limited by cue, ace finds rest

indicators.note: something limited by another is bounded by it on both sides, so it sits within

parts.note: a cue is a prompt, a reminder of what to do or say
A is the abbreviation for ace in cards

explanation.surface: A snooker ace, hampered by their cue, has a rest.
explanation.walkthrough: Cue, ace and rest all suggest snooker, where the rest is a cue support; here the cue is a prompt and rest means what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: The rest of something is what is left over once part has gone, which is its remainder.

clue.text: Safely negotiate dire clue?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to come through a storm or crisis without harm
second meaning: read as an instruction to rework four letters, it is a clue whose solution would be 'dire'

explanation.surface: Getting safely through a horribly difficult crossword clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer read as a cryptic clue means 'rearrange R-I-D-E', which yields DIRE; the question mark flags this reverse trick.
explanation.definitionFit: To ride out a storm or crisis is to come through it without serious harm, getting past it safely.

clue.text: Suggested, with humour, covering T. Rex within limits

indicators.note: to cover something is to lie over and around it, enclosing it

parts.note: humour as in a frame of mind, a mood
taken as written

indicators.note: keeping only what lies within the limits drops the edges and leaves the middle

parts.note: the middle letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone jokingly proposed a dinosaur exhibit with boundaries round the T. Rex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'T. Rex' is split: the T stands as written and only the inside of 'Rex' is kept.
explanation.definitionFit: To moot an idea is to raise it for discussion, so mooted means put forward or proposed.

clue.text: Race cut short, feeling in one's bones returning and worsening

indicators.note: something cut short loses its end, so the final letter goes

parts.note: a relay is a race run in legs by a team

indicators.note: returning means going back the way it came, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: ESP, extrasensory perception, an intuition felt in one's bones

explanation.surface: A runner's race ended early as an aching in their bones came back and got worse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Feeling in one's bones' looks like literal pain; it is an intuitive hunch, the sixth sense ESP.
explanation.definitionFit: A relapse is a deterioration after a period of improvement, especially in illness, so it names a worsening.

clue.text: Fancy knight and my boss getting mentioned in the same breath!

parts.note: to fancy something is to like it
N is the chess notation for knight
the setter's boss is the crossword editor, ED

explanation.surface: Someone is delighted that their boss and a knight are spoken of together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My boss' is the setter speaking: a crossword setter answers to the editor, ED. 'Fancy' looks like an exclamation of surprise but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Two things mentioned in the same breath are being compared or treated as equals, which is what likened means.

clue.text: General, top of the pecking order?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: taking everything into account, as an adjective
second meaning, read as two words: someone placed above everyone else

explanation.surface: A general sits at the top of the military pecking order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'General' looks like the army rank; it is the adjective. The question mark flags the split into two words for the second reading.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means taken as a whole, while split it describes one ranked above everyone, which sits at the top.

clue.text: Pick softer version of drug?

parts.note: E is slang for the drug ecstasy
lite is the marketing spelling for a milder, lower-strength product

explanation.surface: Someone choosing a milder form of a drug.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'lite' version of E is read as one word; 'Pick' is the noun, as in the pick of the bunch.
explanation.definitionFit: The pick of a group is its best members, which is what the elite are.

clue.text: Bank investor twisted in the end

indicators.note: a twist at the tail mixes up only the closing letters, leaving the rest in place

parts.note: an angel is a backer who invests in a show or start-up

explanation.surface: A bank's investor went crooked in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bank' suggests finance alongside investor, but it is the verb for tilting an aircraft in a turn.
explanation.definitionFit: When a plane banks it tilts to one side, and to angle something is likewise to set it at a slant.

clue.text: He wrote notes in out-of-court ruling

indicators.note: out of means without here, so the abbreviation for court is taken away

parts.note: a verdict is a court's ruling
CT is the standard abbreviation for court

explanation.surface: A judge or lawyer wrote notes on an out-of-court settlement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out-of-court' looks like a legal settlement, but it says remove CT. 'Notes' are musical notes, not legal ones.
explanation.definitionFit: Giuseppe Verdi was the Italian opera composer, so writing musical notes was his job.

clue.text: Spread out at home with dog lying around, speaking freely

parts.note: to open a map is to spread it out
someone at home is in

indicators.note: something lying around has been turned about, so these letters face the other way

parts.note: a pug is a small breed of dog

explanation.surface: Sprawled at home with the dog lounging nearby, someone talks without inhibition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lying around' paints a lazy dog, but it signals the dog's name turning round.
explanation.definitionFit: Opening up means becoming candid and sharing thoughts or feelings, that is talking openly without holding back.

clue.text: One chasing a lot of wine is for Macron most encouraging

indicators.note: a lot of something is most but not all of it, so the final letter is dropped
one chasing another runs behind it, so it comes after in the sequence

parts.note: rosé is a pink wine
I is the Roman numeral for one
est is French for is, as Macron, the French president, would say it

explanation.surface: Someone who keeps drinking wine is, in Macron's view, the most hopeful sort.
explanation.walkthrough: Macron is France's president, so 'is for Macron' means the French word for is.
explanation.definitionFit: A rosy outlook is hopeful and promising, so the rosiest prospects are the most encouraging ones.

clue.text: Vicar's meeting before worship

indicators.note: two things meeting are joined end to end, one directly after the other

parts.note: Rev, short for Reverend, the title of a vicar; the 's reads as 'is'
ere is an old word for before

explanation.surface: A vicar holds a meeting ahead of the church service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worship' looks like the church service, but it is the verb, to adore.
explanation.definitionFit: To revere someone is to feel deep respect or awe for them, close to worshipping them.
